title: Here’s the Thing: We Could Do Something Else
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Written after sitting on the idea for over a month because it felt risky, Stuart confronts the wave of teachers leaving education during the pandemic year, using a colleague's realization that his teaching-honed skills were transferable to project management as a jumping-off point. He argues that meaning and agency are essential to the human spirit (citing Viktor Frankl), that pandemic teaching had genuinely stripped away a sense of control, but that agency in the work remains real even when it's harder to see. The article's central, deliberately risky claim is that teachers could do something else and still hold their heads high -- other careers carry real dignity and impact too. He insists this isn't an invitation to leave, but a necessary acknowledgment that staying in teaching should be an active, willed choice rather than a trap, because 'teaching, fundamentally, is always that: a choice.'
points: Stuart's most load-bearing (and self-described 'risky') claim: teachers are qualified to do other meaningful work, and choosing to leave education doesn't diminish a person's dignity or impact.

He roots the argument in Viktor Frankl's concentration-camp-forged insight that meaning and agency are essential to enduring hardship, applying it to pandemic-era teachers who felt they'd lost control of their work.

His practical purpose in naming the exit option explicitly is to make staying a willed, examined choice rather than a default born of feeling trapped -- 'teaching, fundamentally, is always that: a choice.'
He proposes a loose personal formula (P = wc², echoing E = mc²) to argue that teaching may carry outsized potential impact, without claiming it's the only path to a meaningful working life.
quotes: There is something deeply injurious to the human spirit about finding ourselves in spots bereft of meaning and agency. You and I were made to matter — and to choose. Viktor Frankl discovered this in a Nazi concentration camp; meaning and agency, he writes, can be found even amidst the harshest brutality.
But the reality of our agency is as durable as ever. It's just become extra good at hiding.
But here it is. The truth is this: you and I could do something else. We could do something besides teaching, besides education. And in doing that, we could still hold our heads high.

But look, the work ahead is going to take whole-souled engagement: intellectually, physically, emotionally, socially, volitionally. In order to fully restore ourselves for such work, I think we each need to grapple with the reality that we don't have to do it.
I think work is kind of like that too — maybe P = wc², in which the (p)otential meaning and impact of a career is equivalent to the (w)ork the career entails times the speed of light squared.
So, look. I'm a person who has spent the last eight years writing blog posts in my spare time for a single driving purpose: I want you to stay in education.

Because for the work to come, we all need to be here because we've chosen to be. Because teaching, fundamentally, is always that: a choice. That's what it was in my classroom today, and that's what it was in yours.
